abstract: One of the earliest described cases of putative homoploid hybrid speciation was 35 years ago for the Australian cotton species, Gossypium bickii. This inference was based on discordance between chloroplast- and nuclear-based phylogenetic reconstructions, a type of incongruence that has become a relatively common observation in plants. Here we reevaluate evidence bearing on the evolutionary history of G. bickii in the context of an expanded sampling of all but one of the 17 described Australian cotton species, using whole-genome resequencing data based on 18,784 single-copy nuclear genes and entire plastome sequences. Genome-wide phylogenomic analyses resolved three well-defined sections (Sturtia, Hibiscoidea and Grandicalyx) and recapitulate the previously reported discordance between nuclear and plastid phylogenies. Although plastome inferences mirror phylogenetic discordance inferred earlier for G. bickii and G. cunninghamii, genome-wide nuclear data did not reveal compelling signals of interspecific introgression, perhaps because of population genetic nuclear swamping by a quantitatively larger paternal population and by subsequent genomic divergence. All analyses, including genome-wide phylogenetics and dating estimation, support a narrative in which there was early and rapid diversification of the three Australian sections, accompanied by early intersectional reticulation of plastomes without residual evidence in the nuclear genome.
